extracted.intended_audience: research funders, research-policy analysts, grant administrators, and researchers studying peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Synthesis and evaluation of the effectiveness, reliability, fairness, burden, and possible reforms of grant peer review processes in the health sciences (and related research funding contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review must fund the 'best' science
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of 'best' science is not fixed; it may include research that is innovative, interdisciplinary and applied. Evaluation should consider whether peer review supports these dimensions of quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that 'best' can vary by funder/objective. The document highlights tensions (originality vs tradition) and notes that criteria emphasising scholarship over impact can bias against high-impact or risky work. Be explicit about which aspects of 'best' the scheme rewards and measure outcomes accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review is probably anti-innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical evidence indicates a bias against innovative or high-risk proposals: novel proposals often score lower even when feasible, possibly because they lack preceding work and require less risk-averse reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations discussed include: using reviewers with different cognitive biases for specific schemes (e.g. specialists in high-risk research), making 'innovation' an explicit assessment criterion, increasing the weight given to innovation, using reviewer disagreement as a signal of novelty, running high-risk/high-reward schemes (e.g. NIH Pioneer), and structured deliberative processes (Delphi). Note trade-offs: panels may lack expertise to assess innovation and weighting innovation can interact with other biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinarity fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unclear whether peer review treats interdisciplinary research fairly; interdisciplinary proposals may be disadvantaged because reviews must combine different understandings of 'quality' and it can be hard to find appropriate peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible remedies include increasing the size and disciplinary breadth of panels and diminishing the role of single in-depth reviewers, but these raise burden and may reduce consistency. Empirical findings (e.g. lower success rates with greater interdisciplinarity) should be monitored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applied research fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review may inhibit translational/applied research because it can prevent iterative development with funders and may undervalue publications in specialist (lower-impact) outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider including research users on panels, evaluating likely impact during review, and using 'merit review panels' that combine academic and user/policy perspectives (noting the risk that considering impact might disadvantage innovation). Empirical evidence on this bias is limited and mixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive validity: peer review as predictor of future performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is at best a weak predictor of future research performance; several studies find little or no association between application rankings and subsequent bibliometric or commercial outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret bibliometric analyses cautiously (they are proxies). Acknowledge limits of prediction beyond identifying top ~20–30% of proposals. Consider using alternative outcome measures and longitudinal evaluation to assess predictive validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability — ratings vary considerably between reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-rater reliabilities are generally low (examples: correlations ~0.19–0.23 in some studies), indicating substantial variability in individual reviewer judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure inter-rater reliability within your system. Remedies include increasing numbers of reviewers per application, reviewer training, evaluating review quality, and considering statistical aggregation methods (e.g. mean reviewer scores) as pragmatic alternatives to lengthy consensus processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisionmaking consistency (acceptable agreement thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is conflicting evidence on whether peer review achieves acceptable consistency; some studies report agreement rates in the 65–83% range while Bornmann suggests 80–90% as an expectation for such decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define acceptable agreement thresholds for your scheme and monitor performance. Use empirical comparisons (e.g. independent panels) to estimate agreement and explore causes of variability. Consider whether panels or alternative procedures meet the predefined threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel discussion effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel meeting discussions often have minimal effects on improving consistency or changing initial reviewer ratings for most applications; some studies find panel discussion changes outcomes for around 10% (or in some cases up to 13%) of applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the marginal benefit of panel discussions versus their cost. Consider alternatives such as relying on mean reviewer scores, initial triage, or targeted discussions for high-disagreement applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer diversity trade-off
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing diversity of background and discipline among reviewers reduces rating consistency; intra-class correlation can be much lower when mixing research, practice, and policy backgrounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the goal of diverse perspectives (which may improve fairness/representativeness) with the need for reliable, consistent scores. Consider deliberate panel design, transparency about trade-offs, and targeted processes (e.g. additional reviewers) for interdisciplinary proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer training and guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Training reviewers can improve reliability and review quality. NIH recommended training focus areas include emphasising strengths, focusing on impact, reviewing merit not rewriting, recognising implicit bias, using benchmark applications, and flagging bias towards lesser-known organisations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement brief, focused training (pilots have shown increases in inter-rater reliability). Provide benchmark/sample applications during panels and refreshers for experienced reviewers. Monitor whether training increases time spent reviewing and whether reliability gains persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate quality of reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Funders often evaluate review quality using criteria such as completeness, level of substantiation, appropriateness, comprehensibility, timeliness and usefulness (European Science Foundation survey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set explicit criteria for review quality, sample or audit reviews, provide feedback to reviewers, and consider returning or rejecting inadequate reviews. Be aware that adding review-evaluation increases system burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness — gender bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence on gender bias in grant review is substantial but conflicting: some studies and meta-analyses find small but detectable male advantage; others find little or no systematic gender bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor gender-disaggregated application and success rates, consider blinding where feasible, and investigate systemic causes (e.g. differences in track records). Use large-scale, carefully controlled analyses before making policy changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness — age and early-career bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence on age bias is mixed. Concerns exist that reliance on prior publications/funding disadvantages early-career researchers; some funders have introduced measures to equalise success rates for new investigators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track success by career stage, consider separate funding streams or adjusted criteria for early-career applicants, and avoid over-weighting prior funding/publication history when that would bias against newcomers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness — cronyism and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: There is evidence that prior affiliation with reviewers or panel membership can increase chances of funding; robust conflict-of-interest (COI) procedures are necessary but may not fully prevent cronyism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain strict COI policies, consider anonymisation/blinding where feasible, monitor outcomes for patterns consistent with cronyism, and be transparent about panel membership and decision processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive particularism
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may favour proposals within their own field or school of thought ('cognitive particularism'), potentially steering funding toward well-understood areas rather than novel directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Countermeasures include broadening the range of problems judged by each group, ensuring diversity of perspectives, and explicitly valuing cross-field or novel approaches. Be mindful that some studies find reviewers may be more critical of proposals in their own expertise area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymisation / blinding of applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Blinding applications can reduce obvious abuses (bias on grounds of race, gender, institution), but anonymisation may be imperfect because applicants can be identified from content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use blinding where it is likely to be effective (e.g. short anonymised versions), evaluate its actual impact (control for changes in application length/content), and combine with other anti-bias measures. Recognise limits in small fields or where identity is inferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can lack accountability (e.g. anonymous reviews reduce transparency); funders are urged to be open about uncertainty and decision processes and to share data to enable evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase transparency by publishing score distributions, making non-sensitive review data available for research, providing applicants with clearer feedback, and documenting decision rationales. Balance transparency with confidentiality and COI concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can slow down grant award processes detrimentally; evidence on the extent of the problem is unclear but timeliness is a recurring concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure review-to-award timelines, set targets, use streamlined/triage procedures to speed decisions, and pilot virtual/accelerated review methods where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of peer review and distribution of costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of peer review is high and increasing, with around 75% falling on applicants (time to prepare applications); many burden-reduction efforts focus on funders/reviewers rather than applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure time and financial costs for applicants and reviewers, consider short application formats with triage, implement accelerated review or lotteries for marginal cases, and redesign processes to reduce repetitive workload on applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of lotteries / random allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing a lottery element for some funding decisions could reduce burden and bias, and allow better evaluation of decision processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider random allocation for proposals judged of comparable merit (e.g. near the funding threshold), pilot with careful evaluation of impacts on fairness, burden, and outcomes, and communicate rationale clearly to stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reviewer uncertainty and score distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: The distribution of scores and reviewer disagreement can be used as an input: high disagreement may indicate potentially innovative but risky research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture and analyse score distributions and explicit measures of reviewer uncertainty; develop decision rules that treat high-disagreement proposals differently (e.g. further review, targeted funding, or weighting disagreement as a positive signal for novelty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting researchers (people-based funding) versus selecting projects
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative to project selection is to select researchers on merit (e.g. fellowships or 'people' awards) and give them freedom to pursue opportunities, which may better support innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use people-based schemes for certain objectives (e.g. high-risk innovation), monitor differences in outcomes versus project-based funding, and consider portfolio approaches combining both models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of virtual panels and remote review
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtual peer review (teleconference, videoconference, virtual worlds) can cut costs and yields scoring similar to face-to-face panels, although participants value in-person social aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot virtual modalities to reduce costs and logistical burdens while monitoring any effects on score distributions, reviewer engagement, and panel dynamics. Consider hybrid approaches where interaction-intensive decisions remain face-to-face.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bibliometrics and alternative metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Bibliometric analyses are imperfect proxies of future performance; studies show weak or no correlation between peer review rankings and bibliometric outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bibliometrics cautiously as supplementary indicators, not sole determinants. Combine quantitative metrics with qualitative expert assessment and validate metrics against relevant outcomes for the funded work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-quality assessment (GRADE-like scale / Box 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The review rates quality of evidence on a scale: 1 Assumptions; 2 Suggestive; 3 Conflicting; 4 Agreement; 5 Compelling. Aggregated strength of evidence should be reported for each criticism area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When synthesising evidence about peer review, explicitly rate the strength and consistency of findings using a defined scale (as above), report uncertainty, and avoid overstating conclusions when evidence is suggestive or conflicting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funders should experiment and share data
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a need for open, transparent experimentation and evaluation of different ways to fund research, requiring data sharing from the funding community to progress knowledge about what works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders should pilot alternative allocation mechanisms (lotteries, streamlined proposals, people-based funding, reviewer training interventions), publish evaluation data (anonymised where necessary), and cooperate with researchers to enable meta-evaluation of funding mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of benchmark applications during panels
rubrics_metrics.description: Using benchmark applications during panel meetings can provide review guidelines and improve consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide panels with exemplars of high-, medium- and low-quality applications as anchors. Include guidance on how to apply benchmarks and periodically refresh exemplars to reflect evolving standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of likely impact as an assessment criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Considering likely impact at the application stage may help evaluate applied research but may disadvantage innovative research; its use is debated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define when impact should be a core criterion (e.g. translational programmes) and when it should be secondary. Be explicit about weighting and the potential trade-offs with innovation.
